profit.title: Profit & loss analysis
profit.description: Compare periods, investigate causes and calculate profit under improvement scenarios.
profit.thinking: Comparing financial, sales and purchasing data…
questions: Compare the previous and current income statements. Identify the three key business anomalies, calculate the changes and explain what needs attention first.
Cross-check product sales and raw-material purchasing data. Why did gross margin fall? Separate facts, reasonable inferences and factors that still need evidence.
With revenue at NT$12 million and operating expenses at NT$2.4 million, what would gross profit and operating profit be at gross margins of 28% and 30%?

turns.intro: Revenue grew, but operating profit fell. Start with a side-by-side comparison.
points: Costs rose 28.6%, faster than revenue at 20%. Gross margin fell from 30% to 25%, a decline of 5 percentage points.
Operating profit fell from NT$1 million to NT$600,000, a drop of NT$400,000.
Expenses rose from NT$2 million to NT$2.4 million. With gross profit unchanged, the extra NT$400,000 directly reduced operating profit.
turns.conclusion: First investigate why costs grew and gross profit did not follow revenue; then review the expense increases and their justification.
evidence: Source: 01 — P&L and product purchasing workbook / Monthly income statement.
Change = (current − previous) ÷ previous. Gross margin = gross profit ÷ revenue: 300 ÷ 1,000 = 30%; 300 ÷ 1,200 = 25%.

turns.intro: Cross-check product margins and material prices. Keep observed facts separate from explanations.

table.caption: Gross margin by product | Results from the supplied demo conversation

points: Steel rose from NT$50/kg to NT$60/kg (+20%); aluminium rose from NT$80/kg to NT$84/kg (+5%).
Inference | Higher material prices may compress margins
Margins for A and B fell as material prices rose. Material costs may be one factor, but their full contribution has not been quantified.
Unknown | Inventory, consumption and other manufacturing costs
Purchasing amounts are not the same as current-period cost of goods sold. Inventory, consumption and cost details are still needed, as is an explanation for the improvement in product C.
turns.conclusion: Check the cost breakdown before evaluating supplier negotiations or alternatives. Material price increases cannot be treated as the complete explanation.
evidence: Sources: product sales comparison in the selected KIP conversation; 01 — P&L and product purchasing workbook / Raw-material purchasing analysis.
Source caveat: inventory, consumption and other manufacturing costs create differences between purchases and cost of goods sold. Do not infer full causation.

turns.intro: Hold revenue at NT$12 million and operating expenses at NT$2.4 million, then compare two gross-margin scenarios.
points: Gross profit: 1,200 × 28% = 336; operating profit: 336 − 240 = 96, an increase of 36 over the current period (all in NT$10,000).
Gross profit: 1,200 × 30% = 360; operating profit: 360 − 240 = 120, an increase of 60 over the current period (all in NT$10,000).
turns.conclusion: With revenue and expenses unchanged, a 30% margin yields NT$240,000 more operating profit than a 28% margin. These are conditional calculations; feasibility still depends on the improvement measures.
evidence: Basis: conditions and results from the third turn of the same KIP demo. Current operating profit is NT$600,000.
Gross profit = revenue × gross margin; operating profit = gross profit − operating expenses. This reproduces sample calculations and is not a live analysis.
